prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which brought atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty and opened new precision tests of gravity and fundamental physics

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks to Katori and Ye. After round 1 the committee is split four to four between B022 and B039, and I have tried to test my own position against the strongest objections instead of counting heads. The scientific core still stands on what can be measured. The magic-wavelength lattice is one specific idea: it cancels the light shift on the clock transition while confining the atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, so first-order Doppler and recoil shifts vanish and many atoms are probed at once. That gives narrow lines, high signal-to-noise and short averaging times, which is what makes a 10^-18 systematic budget something one can actually verify rather than claim. The result has been reproduced by several independent groups (Tokyo/RIKEN, JILA, PTB, NIST, SYRTE), and the comparisons between clocks are themselves the experimental evidence. In answer to the chair's question on what new fact about nature has been delivered beyond a smaller error bar: the gravitational redshift has been resolved across millimetre-scale height differences within one atomic sample, which is a test of general relativity in a regime no earlier instrument reached; limits on drifting fundamental constants and on dark-matter couplings have been tightened by clock comparisons; and the clock itself has become a many-body system in which interaction and spin-exchange effects were observed and then controlled. On credit, the division is clean. Katori originated the magic-wavelength lattice proposal and its first demonstration with strontium; Ye's group carried the concept to the accuracy and stability records and the many-body and redshift results. Remove either name and the citation no longer describes the achievement. For the Secretary's question on the SI second: the redefinition is a consequence of this result and not a condition for it. The measurements are done and independent, and I would not tie a scientific judgement to a metrology committee's calendar.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 prize (Hall and Hansch, frequency comb and laser precision spectroscopy) and the 2012 prize (Wineland and Haroche, control of single quantum systems, including ion clocks) is a real reservation and I do not think it can be argued away; it can only be answered by wording. A citation that says 'optical clocks' would reopen both prizes, whereas one that names magic-wavelength lattice trapping and the accuracy it enabled identifies a distinct step. I also accept the point made by Danielsson, Eriksson, Johansson and Mehlig that a clock is first of all a measurement capability, and that topological insulators supplied a new organising principle for matter. That is a genuine difference in kind between the two candidates, and a committee that weights conceptual novelty above metrological reach could reasonably pick B039. Finally, credit outside the two names (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Hollberg and the single-ion groups with their own competitive Al+ and Yb+ clocks) has not been independently verified by me and should be checked with external experts before the final ballot.

responses.point: Danielsson asks what new fact about the world a lattice clock has delivered beyond a smaller error bar, and says that a clock is a superb measurement that does not yet show nature doing something unexpected.
responses.response: I take the question as the right test and I think the record answers it, though not with a single dramatic surprise. Resolving the gravitational redshift across millimetres inside one sample is a new observation, and it was possible only because the lattice holds thousands of atoms with very small systematic shifts. The many-body clock physics (interaction shifts, spin-exchange and their suppression) was an unexpected effect that the lattice geometry revealed, and it now guides the design of the best clocks. The bounds on drifting constants and dark-matter couplings are new measurements about nature, not repetitions of older ones. I agree that the 2D and 3D topological story is a bigger conceptual change. My disagreement is only that 'what the instrument saw' should count as much as 'what the theory predicted' when the observations are new. I also note he has kept B022 as his first alternative, so we may be closer on the ballot than on the ranking.

responses.point: Mehlig says that if the committee weights measurement precision above conceptual novelty then B022 wins, and warns against letting an anticipated metrological decision such as the redefinition of the second drive the prize.
responses.response: I agree that the redefinition should not drive the decision, and I would go further and say it should not be mentioned as a reason in the citation. It is a consequence, and the case rests on the 10^-18 comparisons already published. On weighting, I do not think the choice is only precision versus novelty. The lattice clock is a new way of making a quantum measurement, with a many-atom, Doppler-free and recoil-free design, and the novelty is in the design principle. Where I accept his point is that this is a different kind of novelty from band topology and the committee must decide openly which kind it values. I would not call B039 an unreasonable first choice, and I want my case judged on the evidence and not on the number of members who share it.

responses.point: Lindroth asks whether Katori's early strontium demonstration and Ye's accuracy record are both needed in the citation, and notes that if one is doubtful the two-person claim becomes less obvious.
responses.response: I looked at that question again and I think both are needed, for different reasons. Without Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice demonstration there is no concept to credit. Without the Ye group's work the concept would be a good idea with an unproven accuracy, and the 10^-18 level, the clock-comparison results and the many-body studies are what show it opens a new regime. I would keep the two names and write the citation as 'invention and realisation' so that each contribution is present. I agree with her that the citation should lean on the physics exposed (redshift, constants, dark matter) and not on the fact that the numbers are small, and I have changed my citation to say so.

responses.point: Eriksson says that cleaner credit alone does not make B022 stronger science, and that the 2D quantum spin Hall effect alone could look arbitrary against the later 3D topological insulator discovery.
responses.response: I agree that credit clarity is not a scientific argument, and I do not rest on it. It is a tiebreaker only once the science is judged comparable, and the committee must judge that. I also take her point about 2D versus 3D seriously, and it is the reason I keep B039 as my first alternative and not a distant one. My difficulty is with a prize that is defensible only if one reads the priority history in a particular way: the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal is what directed the HgTe experiment, and Zhang's death removes an option for the committee but does not remove the objection. If external experts tell us the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio is a fair reading of the decisive steps, and that the 3D work is a separate achievement not stranded by the prize, I would find B039 considerably easier to support.

responses.point: Olsson says the citation should be written around the magic-wavelength lattice and the resulting accuracy so that the record shows what is new, and shares my concern about credit outside the two names.
responses.response: I agree and have tightened the citation in that direction: 'invention and realisation', 'magic-wavelength trapping', and the 10^-18 level are all in the wording, and neither 'frequency standard' alone nor 'optical clock' alone appears as the claim. On the credit concern, I think the honest position is that we cannot verify the Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and Hollberg contributions from the files we hold, so the Secretary should ask external experts to review the priority chronology for B022 before the final ballot, as the chair proposes. I would accept the outcome of that review even if it complicates a prize I prefer.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize as leaving room for a further precision-timekeeping prize, which a citation can only partly resolve.

Whether the committee accepts new observational capability (millimetre-scale redshift, many-body clock physics, constraints on constants and dark matter) as the equivalent of a conceptual discovery; this is the real hinge between B022 and B039.

Priority and credit among contributors outside the two names, including early Sr, Yb and Hg lattice work and the single-ion clock groups, which I cannot verify from the supplied files and which external experts should check.

If B022 does not succeed, whether B039 can be worded to the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators with the HgTe realisation without stranding the 3D work or the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal.
statement.conflict_note: No decisive conflict. I record again that I spent part of my PhD period in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder and that Jun Ye is at JILA, so there is a loose lineage and community link to the clock field; I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye and no stake in either. I would accept a formal recusal ruling if the committee thinks the Hall lineage warrants one for B022, and I note that the 2005 prize to Hall is part of the overlap question I discuss above. I also work in atomic physics at Lund and have been involved in WACQT, which is relevant only if B005, B025 or B023 are discussed.
